key_claims: taVNS is a promising non-invasive neuromodulation approach for disorders of consciousness, but evidence is preliminary.

Mechanistic models suggest taVNS may influence consciousness via the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, engaging brainstem nuclei and modulating cortical networks, but this is a working model, not a validated causal pathway.

Preliminary data suggest patients in minimally conscious state may respond more often than those with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome/vegetative state, but the only sham-controlled randomized trial found no significant overall between-group difference.
Multimodal tools like EEG, fNIRS, heart rate variability, and serum biomarkers may improve understanding and responder stratification, but integrated evidence within same cohorts is scarce.

taVNS appears promising as an adjunctive intervention, but routine clinical application remains provisional until ongoing trials clarify efficacy, durability, optimal parameters, and responder profiles.
limitations: Evidence is limited by small samples, protocol heterogeneity, and short follow-up.
The review is narrative, not systematic, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis was performed.
Direct evidence for the proposed mechanisms in DoC patients is incomplete; much is indirect from other populations or animal studies.
The only sham-controlled randomized trial found no significant overall between-group difference.
what_not_to_say: taVNS is an established or proven treatment for disorders of consciousness.
taVNS has been shown to cause recovery of consciousness.
The proposed mechanisms are validated causal pathways.
taVNS is effective for all DoC patients.
The review provides quantitative evidence of efficacy.
